The largest documented specimens of Norway redfish (Sebastes viviparus) reach a total length of 66.5 centimeters [Li = 66.5 centimeters], placing this species among the smaller members of the genus, which includes commercially important congeners exceeding 100 centimeters. Most field surveys have recorded individuals up to approximately 55 centimeters, with the maximum value representing the upper extreme of the size distribution, likely achieved only by old females in favorable environments. The body form is deep and robust, typical of demersal scorpaenids, and the species displays a reddish coloration that deepens with age. Adult body mass shows considerable variation, with the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual estimated at 4100 grams [Wwi = 4100 grams], based on length-weight regressions compiled from coastal Norwegian waters. This close correspondence between length and mass follows a power-law relationship that reflects the species’ stocky body plan, with most reproductive females weighing between 2500 and 3500 grams in the central North Sea. Sexual dimorphism in size is modest, though females tend to attain slightly larger asymptotic dimensions than males, a pattern common among viviparous teleosts where maternal body volume directly limits brood space.

Onset of reproductive activity in Sebastes viviparus is triggered by the attainment of a total length of 12.5 centimeters [Lp = 12.5 centimeters], which corresponds to approximately three to four years of age in Norwegian coastal populations. This length at first maturity is relatively low within the genus, reflecting the species’ adaptation to cooler, less productive shelf ecosystems where early reproduction conveys a selective advantage. Puberty is closely tied to somatic growth rate, with faster-growing individuals reaching the critical size threshold earlier than those experiencing slower growth under suboptimal feeding conditions. Histological examination of gonadal tissue reveals that vitellogenesis begins shortly after females surpass this length, and the first successful spawning typically occurs in the subsequent autumn. Mature females produce a single large batch of eggs each winter, fertilized internally by males who also mature at a slightly smaller size, around 10.0 centimeters. Exploitation by trawl fisheries can reduce the mean size of the spawning stock, potentially lowering the proportion of first-time spawners that successfully contribute to recruitment.

The maximum reproductive rate of Norway redfish under ambient thermal conditions at 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C] has been reported as one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], with females producing between 20000 and 50000 live young per brood [N_R_i = between 20000 and 50000 live young per brood]. This annual output is considerable for a fish of this body size but is constrained by the viviparous mode of reproduction, in which developing embryos are retained and nourished internally for several months before parturition. Gestation extends from late autumn through early spring, and the larvae are released as free-swimming, exogenously feeding individuals measuring about 6 millimeters in length, a relatively advanced stage compared to the pelagic eggs of most marine teleosts. Litter size scales positively with maternal length, and the largest females can produce up to 120000 offspring in a single reproductive event under prolonged cold conditions. The trade-off between offspring number and size is apparent in this species, as larvae must be sufficiently developed at release to survive the early spring plankton bloom.

The wet weight of a newly fertilized ovum, before the start of embryonic development, is approximately 0.0016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0016 grams], based on the average egg dimensions of 2.0 millimeters in length and 1.25 millimeters in width. This value, derived from the formula for a prolate spheroid, yields an egg mass that is somewhat larger than that observed in oviparous scorpaenids, reflecting the increased per-offspring investment typical of viviparous species. The yolky egg is buoyant but slightly negatively buoyant, settling onto the substrate shortly after fertilization, though in captivity the ova are often found adhering to artificial structures. After a gestation period of approximately 8 to 9 weeks at 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C], yolk-sac larvae hatch, weighing slightly less than the egg due to metabolic consumption of yolk reserves during development. The relatively large egg size ensures that hatchlings possess sufficient endogenous nutrition to survive through the first days of exogenous feeding, a critical period in the early life history of this species. Field collections indicate that larval growth during the yolk-sac stage is rapid, with larvae doubling in length within the first week post-eclosion.

Longevity in Sebastes viviparus has been estimated at 40 years [am = 40 years] based on otolith readings from populations inhabiting the cold waters of the Norwegian Sea at a mean annual temperature of 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C]. This lengthy lifespan, equivalent to approximately 14600 days, is characteristic of many Sebastes species and reflects a slow-growth, late-maturing life-history strategy that buffers populations against years of poor recruitment. Age validation using bomb radiocarbon dating has confirmed that certain individuals from deep fjord environments exceed the 40-year mark, reaching 45 to 50 years in some records. The exceptionally long reproductive window allows females to produce many broods over their lifetime, compensating for the relatively low fecundity per event compared to batch-spawning teleosts. Senescence appears gradual, with no abrupt decline in reproductive output observed until the final two to three years of life, after which physiological deterioration accelerates. This extended lifespan, coupled with iteroparous reproduction, makes the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as removal of older age classes disproportionately impacts future recruitment.
